nodes.content: Design a session-typed language supporting endpoint delegation and structured cancellation without stranded peers or broken protocol guarantees.
requirements: Establish protocol safety and cancellation progress under fair scheduling and reliable asynchronous delivery.
Under separate compilation, accept 12 valid delegation-and-cancellation programs and reject 12 protocol-invalid variants.

nodes.content: Combine affine delegation, cancel-labelled session transitions, and acknowledged scope-wide cancellation over ownership graphs; publish effect-annotated interfaces for separate compilation.
When cancellation races with in-flight delegation, which owner must acknowledge the peer’s cancel transition before the scope can close?
Assigning cancellation responsibility to the sender until transfer acknowledgement, then the receiver, prevents missing acknowledgements during delegation races.
Specify ownership handoff rules, model-check delegation races, and prove each cancel acknowledgement has exactly one responsible owner.
Model-check 48 two-hop delegation/cancellation interleavings in TLA+ with reliable FIFO queues, recording orphaned acknowledgements and duplicate owners.
Across 48 bounded TLA+ interleavings, orphaned acknowledgements and duplicate owners were both zero; every cancellation reached an accountable owner.
Adopt acknowledgement-gated ownership transfer for the prototype; bounded checks found no orphaned acknowledgements or duplicate owners.
DelegationCancel.tla and TLC.cfg encode two-hop handoffs, FIFO cancellation, and invariants for orphaned acknowledgements and duplicate owners.
Extend DelegationCancel.tla to three-hop transfers with weakly fair delivery and processing; check eventual scope closure and unique acknowledgement ownership.
A fair three-hop trace lets B exit after C acknowledges delegation, leaving A’s pending cancellation unforwarded and scope closure blocked.
Keeping former owners as cancellation forwarders until scope closure ensures exactly one current owner acknowledges each cancel across three hops.
Add forwarding tombstones to DelegationCancel.tla; model-check three-hop races under weak fairness for unique acknowledgements and eventual scope closure.
With forwarding tombstones, TLC explored 18,432 three-hop states and found zero duplicate acknowledgements or fair nonclosing executions.
Use asynchronous reduction semantics and persistent forwarding tombstones to prove protocol preservation and fair cancellation progress.
Define queue-aware typing and tombstone invariants; prove preservation, peer compatibility, and finite-chain cancellation progress under fair reliable delivery.
Translate DelegationCancel.tla into Coq 8.20 small-step rules and check queue-typing preservation and forwarding-tombstone invariants.
CancelSemantics.v contains Coq 8.20 reduction rules, typed queues, forwarding tombstones, and checked preservation and ownership-invariant proofs.
In Coq 8.20, attempt fair-progress proof for CancelSemantics.v, checking whether finite forwarding chains and persistent tombstones prevent stranded peers.
A fair infinite-redelegation trace delivers every cancellation hop but never reaches a stable owner; persistent tombstones alone cannot ensure closure.
Can an epoch-stamped cancellation barrier stop infinite redelegation without rejecting handoffs already in flight?
Epoch-stamped barriers reject newly initiated transfers while draining pre-barrier handoffs; finite in-flight queues then guarantee cancellation closure under fairness.
Add barrier epochs to transfer rules, prove pre-barrier handoffs drain, then derive cancellation progress without assuming a finite delegation chain.
Extend CancelSemantics.v with epoch barriers; check handoff-drain and cancellation-closure lemmas under weak fairness and reliable delivery.
Coq checks epoch-barrier handoff drainage and cancellation closure for finite initial queues under weak fairness and reliable delivery.
CancelSemantics.v now includes epoch-stamped transfer rules and machine-checked preservation, peer compatibility, handoff-drain, and cancellation-closure lemmas.
Extend DelegationCancel.tla using CancelSemantics.v’s epoch rules; model-check four-hop races for queue compatibility and fair scope closure.
TLC explored 61,208 four-hop states with epoch barriers: zero queue-compatibility violations and zero fair nonclosing traces.
Compile modules against sealed session interfaces recording endpoint ownership, delegation permissions, and cancellation effects; link-check duality without source access.
Which interface obligations let separately compiled modules verify forwarding tombstones and epoch barriers when endpoints cross module boundaries?
Publishing affine transfer receipts, tombstone-forwarding effects, and monotone barrier epochs lets linkers reject cross-module cancellation mismatches.
Build the SepCancel-24 corpus: separately compile 12 valid and 12 invalid modules against receipt, tombstone, and epoch interfaces.
SepCancel-24 accepted 12/12 valid programs but rejected only 11/12 invalid variants; one reused an abstract receipt across modules.
Generative, scope-indexed receipt identities with linker-checked single consumption prevent cross-module reuse while preserving tombstone and epoch obligations.
Implement generative receipt IDs and linker consumption checks; rerun SepCancel-24 with separate module compilation and unchanged fixtures.
SepCancel-24 now accepts 12/12 valid and rejects 12/12 invalid programs; the reused receipt fails linker single-consumption checks.
Generate 96 receipt-alias and link-order mutations from SepCancel-24; test linker rejection across module permutations after the receipt fix.
Across 96 mutations, the linker accepted 2 invalid re-exported receipt aliases under reversed link order, violating global single consumption.
How should the linker canonicalize re-exported receipt aliases so single-consumption checks remain invariant under module link order?
Canonicalizing receipt aliases by origin before link-time consumption checks rejects re-exported duplicates regardless of module link order.
Record immutable receipt origins in interfaces, normalize re-export chains before linking, then rerun SepCancel-24 and all 96 mutations.
Patch the SepCancel-24 linker to canonicalize receipt origins across re-exports; rerun 24 fixtures and 96 link-order mutations.
Origin canonicalization preserved SepCancel-24’s 12/12 valid accepts and 12/12 invalid rejects; all 96 mutations were rejected.
Ship origin-canonicalized receipts: baseline tests passed, earlier link-order aliases were caught, and all 96 mutations were rejected.
Implement an epoch-barrier runtime with FIFO queues and receipt-aware forwarding; validate traces against Coq semantics and SepCancel-24.
Build a receipt-aware FIFO runtime, compare its traces against CancelSemantics.v, and run SepCancel-24 under fair-delivery stress.
Implement CancelRT 0.1 with FIFO delivery, epoch-barrier draining, receipt-aware handoffs, and forwarding tombstones following CancelSemantics.v.
CancelRT 0.1 provides bounded FIFO mailboxes, epoch-barrier draining, receipt-indexed delegation, persistent forwarding tombstones, and transition logging.
Replay 10,000 seeded CancelRT 0.1 traces against CancelSemantics.v and execute SepCancel-24 under fair FIFO delivery.
All 10,000 CancelRT traces matched Coq transitions; SepCancel-24 completed 12/12 valid programs and rejected 12/12 invalid variants.
Use CancelRT 0.1 as the reference runtime after 10,000 conforming traces and complete SepCancel-24 results.
Establish an end-to-end refinement contract linking sealed interfaces, linker receipts, CancelRT traces, and Coq progress for composed modules.
How can bounded CancelRT mailboxes refine Coq’s asynchronous queues when backpressure delays cancellation behind in-flight delegation?
Reserving a cancellation slot, interrupting blocked sends, and merging messages by sequence number preserves FIFO refinement despite backpressure.
Inject cancellation at saturated 8-message CancelRT mailboxes; compare merged delivery traces with Coq FIFO semantics and check fair closure.
At mailbox capacity 8, one saturated-send trace deadlocked: its holder awaited space while the receiver awaited a cancellation barrier.
Route barriers through an independent control lane; wake blocked senders and drain committed messages by sequence before closing.
Patch CancelRT with a separate barrier lane; replay 8-slot saturation traces against Coq, checking sender wakeups and fair closure.
With the separate barrier lane, 2,048 saturated-mailbox schedules produced zero deadlocks or Coq trace mismatches.
Prove a Coq stuttering simulation for CancelRT’s control lane and 8-slot queues, including blocked-send wakeups and barrier drainage.
Coq counterexample: a blocked send reserves sequence 9 before enqueue; cancellation aborts it, leaving barrier drainage waiting forever.
Assign sequence numbers only when enqueue commits; barrier drainage tracks committed messages, so aborted blocked sends create no gaps.
Move sequence allocation to enqueue commit, retain the tested control lane, and reprove simulation against the gap counterexample.
Patch CancelRT to number committed enqueues only; replay the sequence-9 counterexample and 2,048 saturated-mailbox schedules.
The sequence-9 gap no longer occurs; all 2,048 saturated-mailbox schedules close with zero Coq trace mismatches.
CancelRT 0.2 replaces pre-enqueue numbering with commit-time sequence allocation and adds the independent cancellation control lane.
Prove CancelRT 0.2’s stuttering simulation in Coq, including commit-time numbering, blocked-send aborts, and fair barrier drainage.
Coq checks CancelRT 0.2’s stuttering simulation and fair closure for finite committed queues; aborted sends leave no sequence gaps.
Adopt CancelRT 0.2’s control lane and commit-time numbering: saturated tests pass, and Coq proves fair closure for finite queues.
